Main_Event_Annotation: Described as the extratropical remnants of the 1900 Galveston hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: Rainfall amounts peaked at 4.25 in with many stations recording over 1 in, suggesting a risk of flood conditions.

Time_Annotation: June 14, 1906 — The remnants of a tropical storm produce light rain across southeastern parts of the state; accumulations reach 0.4–0.5 in.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Light rain was reported across southeastern parts of the state (Wisconsin).
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of a tropical storm.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall (0.4–0.5 in) was observed with no significant hazardous impact.

Time_Annotation: October 19–20, 1916 — The remnants of a hurricane produce rainfall across the state, reaching 1.5–2 in in southeastern counties.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Rainfall was produced across the state, notably in southeastern counties of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the remnants of a hurricane, implying an extratropical transition.
Hazards_Annotation: While measurable rainfall (1.5–2 in) was recorded, no explicit hazardous effects were mentioned.

Time_Annotation: June 26, 1921 — It brought less than 0.75 inches to the entire state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation affected the entire state of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Inferred as part of the tropical cyclone events affecting Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: With less than 0.75 inches of rain reported, no hazardous conditions were described.

Time_Annotation: October 17-18-19, 1923 — It dropped over 2 inches precipitation to southeastern Wisconsin.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation was concentrated in southeastern Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Inferred from context as a tropical cyclone remnant event.
Hazards_Annotation: Despite over 2 inches of rain falling, no explicit hazardous impacts were noted.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Slippery roads led to a car hydroplaning into an embankment, injuring the two occupants.

Time_Annotation: September 24–25, 1941 — The entire state received precipitation with the southeast corner of the state recording up to 1.5 inches.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The precipitation affected all of Wisconsin, with the southeast corner noted specifically.
Main_Event_Annotation: Assumed as part of the series of tropical cyclone events impacting the state.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only noted rainfall without mentioning any associated hazards.

Time_Annotation: October 1949 Texas hurricane — Extratropical remnants of the Category 2 hurricane traversed the state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The extratropical remnants traversed the state of Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Explicitly described as extratropical remnants of a Category 2 hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: No specific hazardous conditions were detailed beyond the storm’s passage.

Time_Annotation: 1960 Texas tropical storm — Peak rainfall of 2.83 in at the Eau Pleine Reservoir.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event impacted areas such as the Eau Pleine Reservoir in Wisconsin.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as a Texas tropical storm impacting Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: Only peak rainfall was noted without mention of additional hazards.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Kenosha County sees extensive damage, with more than 200 homes and 3 businesses flooded; property damage exceeded $6 million.

Property damage exceeded $6 million in Kenosha County.
$900,000 in damage reported across Sheboygan.

Time_Annotation: September 12–14, 1961 — The extratropical remnants of Hurricane Carla brought 54 hours of rainfall to much of the Upper Midwest, with creeks and rivers overtopping their banks and highways experiencing flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Areas such as Brodhead in Wisconsin experienced flooding due to overtopped banks.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the extratropical remnants of Hurricane Carla.
Hazards_Annotation: Flooding on highways and overtopped creeks indicate a clear flood hazard.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: One person was injured when a wall collapsed in Janesville.

Time_Annotation: June 26, 1968 — Rains from Tropical Storm Candy fell across much of Wisconsin, with heavy rains elevating streams and high winds downing power lines.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Central Appleton, Milwaukee, and other parts of Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Directly identified as Tropical Storm Candy.
Hazards_Annotation: Reports of flooding basements and elevated streams coupled with high winds causing power outages confirm both flood and wind hazards.

Total_Summary_Damage.Total_Damage_Annotation: Property damage associated with the event totals $8,000.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Property damage associated with the event totals $8,000.

Time_Annotation: August 21, 1983 – The remnants of Hurricane Alicia combined with a warm front to produce widespread rainfall and moderate winds.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Northeastern Wisconsin, including areas near Green Bay, Milwaukee, and Kenosha, were noted.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event is identified as the remnants of Hurricane Alicia.
Hazards_Annotation: Damaging winds (up to 38 mph and downing trees and power lines) were highlighted.

Time_Annotation: Hurricane Juan1985 — Peak rainfall of 4.9 in in Marinette.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Marinette in Wisconsin experienced significant rainfall.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Hurricane Juan, a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only mentions peak rainfall without detailing additional hazards.

Time_Annotation: September 24–26, 1986 — The remnants of Eastern Pacific Hurricane Newton brought heavy rain that exacerbated flooding, along with severe thunderstorms and downbursts.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southern portions of Wisconsin, including Beloit, Kenosha County, and Sheboygan, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Newton.
Hazards_Annotation: Heavy rain led to flooding while downbursts and severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds.

Time_Annotation: September 20–21, 1988 — The extratropical remnants of Hurricane Gilbert crossed southeastern Wisconsin with rainfall not exceeding 1 in.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin was the primary area mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the extratropical remnants of Hurricane Gilbert.
Hazards_Annotation: Rainfall was light (not exceeding 1 in), and no hazardous effects were described.

Time_Annotation: August 4, 1989 — Following the dissipation of Hurricane Chantal's surface circulation, its remnant cloud shield produced significant precipitation accompanied by severe thunderstorms, damaging winds, and hail.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Regions such as Port Washington, La Crosse, and Janesville in Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Hurricane Chantal after its surface circulation dissipated.
Hazards_Annotation: Damaging winds (up to 75 mph) and hail up to 2.25 in in diameter were reported, leading to structural and tree damage.

Time_Annotation: September 25–27, 1992 — Dual rain events from the remnants of Pacific Hurricane Lester affected the entire state.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The entire state of Wisconsin was subject to the rainfall events.
Main_Event_Annotation: Linked to the remnants of Hurricane Lester.
Hazards_Annotation: Only rainfall was noted without further hazardous conditions.

Time_Annotation: September 14–15, 1998 — Light to moderate rain accompanied the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Frances.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Darlington in Wisconsin was specifically mentioned for rainfall accumulations.
Main_Event_Annotation: Characterized as the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Frances.
Hazards_Annotation: The event reported only light to moderate rain without further hazardous impacts.

Time_Annotation: July 16–17, 2005 — The slow-moving remnants of Hurricane Dennis brought very light rain to parts of Wisconsin amid ongoing drought conditions.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas include parts of Wisconsin such as Phelps.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Dennis.
Hazards_Annotation: Very light rain was recorded, and despite the backdrop of drought, no additional hazards were described.

Time_Annotation: September 4–5, 2008 — Heavy rains accompanied the passage of former Hurricane Gustav, with accumulations reaching 3.14 in and localized ponding affecting roads.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Particularly, Kenosha in southeastern Wisconsin experienced these conditions.
Main_Event_Annotation: Referred to as the passage of former Hurricane Gustav.
Hazards_Annotation: Localized ponding and the potential for flooding in low-lying areas were noted.

Time_Annotation: September 15, 2008 — Light rainfall occurred in far southeastern parts of the state with the passage of former Hurricane Ike.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Far southeastern areas of Wisconsin, including Kenosha, were mentioned.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event was associated with the passage of former Hurricane Ike.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall was reported without any significant hazardous outcomes.

Time_Annotation: September 2–3, 2012 — The remnants of Hurricane Isaac brought negligible rainfall to extreme southeastern Wisconsin, failing to alleviate drought conditions.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Extreme southeastern Wisconsin is noted as the affected region.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as the remnants of Hurricane Isaac.
Hazards_Annotation: Negligible rainfall was observed, with no hazardous effects described.

Time_Annotation: October 30–31, 2012 — A tight pressure gradient between the remnants of Hurricane Sandy and a high-pressure area produced gusty winds and minor beach erosion along Lake Michigan’s coast.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Coastal areas along Lake Michigan from Sheboygan to Kenosha in Wisconsin were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The event was driven by the remnants of Hurricane Sandy.
Hazards_Annotation: Gusty winds—with sustained speeds of 25–30 mph and gusts up to 55 mph—were reported, causing minor beach erosion.

Time_Annotation: May 30–31, 2018 — As a tropical cyclone progressing unusually far inland, Tropical Depression Alberto brought light rainfall to the eastern side.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event impacted regions in Wisconsin as the system progressed inland.
Main_Event_Annotation: Identified as Tropical Depression Alberto, part of the tropical cyclone family.
Hazards_Annotation: Only light rainfall was reported, with no additional hazardous conditions noted.

Time_Annotation: October 26–27, 2019 — The fast-moving extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Olga brought light rainfall as it traversed Lake Michigan.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin, particularly near Kenosha, experienced the effects of the system.
Main_Event_Annotation: Noted as the extratropical remnant of Tropical Storm Olga.
Hazards_Annotation: The report only mentions light rainfall without significant hazardous impacts.

Time_Annotation: June 9–10, 2020 — The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal traversed the state, with widespread rainfall, record wind gusts, and isolated flash flooding.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: West‐central Wisconsin, including areas near Madison and Augusta, were affected.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system transitioned into an extratropical cyclone as it impacted Wisconsin.
Hazards_Annotation: Isolated flash flooding and wind gusts (up to 51 mph) were reported, indicating both flood and wind hazards.

Time_Annotation: July 9, 2024 - The remnants of Hurricane Beryl brought rainfall in Southeastern Wisconsin.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Southeastern Wisconsin is noted as the primary affected region.
Main_Event_Annotation: Attributed to the remnants of Hurricane Beryl.
Hazards_Annotation: The report mentions rainfall only, without additional hazardous details.
